what_it_does: Modern CPUs include 'hardware prefetchers' — small circuits that watch your program's memory access patterns and speculatively fetch data into the fast on-chip cache before the program asks for it, so it arrives sooner. These prefetchers maintain internal tables that remember recent access patterns (for example, detecting that a program reads memory addresses that increase by a fixed stride). Prior research showed that this internal state is not wiped when the CPU switches between different processes or privilege levels, so a malicious observer process can infer what addresses a victim was accessing — a privacy leak. ShadowLoad goes further: it demonstrates that an attacker can actively write crafted memory sequences to deliberately manipulate those prefetcher tables, planting a specific pattern. When the victim process runs next, the pre-loaded prefetcher state causes it to speculatively load data into the cache that it did not ask for, revealing information about the victim's behavior or enabling a covert signaling channel between attacker and victim. This attack crosses process boundaries, user-versus-kernel boundaries, and even the walls of hardware security enclaves — all without any software vulnerability in the victim.
